result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. title: >- [Graph.maximum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the maximum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L68340-L68479){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.maximum_spanning_tree( weight_attr=None, return_subgraph=True, include=None, exclude=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximum spanning tree](../assets/graphs/maximum-spanning-tree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same weighted graph as the minimum spanning tree figure. The maximum spanning tree keeps the heaviest edges that still form a tree: D–E (7), B–E (6), A–D (5), and C–D (3), in the accent color. The card lists them and their total weight, 7 + 6 + 5 + 3 = 21." width="100%"} A maximum spanning tree is a subset of edges that connects all nodes with the maximum total edge weight, without forming any cycle. It is computed exactly like `minimum_spanning_tree()`, except that Kruskal's algorithm considers the edges from heaviest to lightest, keeping each edge that joins two not-yet-connected parts of the tree. When edge weights measure *strength* (similarity, interaction frequency, bandwidth, correlation) rather than cost, the maximum spanning tree keeps the strongest possible set of links that still reaches every node. Common uses include: - extracting the backbone of a dense similarity or correlation network - finding the highest-capacity routes that connect every site (the path between two nodes in the tree maximizes its weakest link) - building tree-structured models from pairwise scores, such as Chow-Liu trees Edge direction is ignored, so on a directed graph the result is a spanning tree of the underlying undirected graph (the chosen edges keep their original orientation). If the graph is disconnected, the result is a maximum spanning *forest*: one tree per connected component. Self-loops are never selected. The original graph is not modified. With `include=` and `exclude=`, the tree is the heaviest one that uses every included edge and none of the excluded ones (NetworkX's `partition_spanning_tree()` with `minimum=False`). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as the weight. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (edges on an unweighted graph count as `1.0`, so any spanning tree is maximal). If a name is given, every edge must hold a number under it; `"weight"` names the weight field. [return_subgraph]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), returns a new `Graph` containing every node of the original graph and only the tree edges. If `False`, returns the selected edges as `(source_id, target_id, weight)` tuples in the order Kruskal's algorithm picked them, from heaviest to lightest (included edges first). [include]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges the tree must contain, as edge IDs or `(u, v)` node pairs (a pair stands for every edge between the two nodes, in either direction). They must not form a cycle. [exclude]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges the tree must not contain, given the same way. Excluding edges can disconnect the graph, in which case the result is a spanning forest. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph or list[tuple[int, int, float]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_subgraph=` is `True`: a new `Graph` with the same directedness and weighting, every node of the original (same IDs, labels and attributes) and the tree edges (same IDs, weights and attributes). If `return_subgraph=` is `False`: a list of `(source_id, target_id, weight)` tuples, the weight being the value the tree was built with (the `weight_attr=` attribute when one is named). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the included edges contain a cycle, an edge is both included and excluded, an edge or node pair in `include=`/`exclude=` does not exist, (with constraints) an edge value is NaN, or `weight_attr=` names an attribute that an edge lacks or holds as a non-number. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Same Kruskal pipeline as `minimum_spanning_tree()` with the weight comparator reversed (equivalently, running MST on $-w$), so cost is $O(E \log E)$ and correctness follows from the cut and cycle properties applied to the negated weights. The construction is a standard tool for extracting a network *backbone*: retain the strongest relationships in a social graph, the highest-throughput links in a communication network, or the most similar species in a hierarchical clustering. Behaves exactly like the minimum variant on disconnected input, yielding one maximum spanning tree per component. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this triangle, a spanning tree only needs 2 of the 3 edges, so the maximum spanning tree keeps the two heaviest ones and drops the lightest: ::: {#b5ab71ba .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 3.0), ("C", "A", 2.0)]) max_st = g.maximum_spanning_tree() # Returns 5.0 (chooses the edges with weights 3.0 and 2.0, dropping 1.0) sum(max_st.get_edge(eid).weight for eid in max_st.get_edge_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5.0 ``` ::: ::: In a similarity network, the maximum spanning tree keeps the strongest tie that attaches each item. Listing the kept edges (via `return_subgraph=False`) shows the backbone, heaviest first; the weak `cat-car` and `dog-truck` links are dropped: ::: {#2451c85f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} sim = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_nodes(["cat", "dog", "car", "truck"]) .add_edges( [ ("cat", "dog", 0.9), ("car", "truck", 0.8), ("dog", "car", 0.2), ("cat", "car", 0.1), ("dog", "truck", 0.15), ] ) ) edges = sim.maximum_spanning_tree(return_subgraph=False) [(sim.get_label_from_id(s), sim.get_label_from_id(t), w) for s, t, w in edges] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [('cat', 'dog', 0.9), ('car', 'truck', 0.8), ('dog', 'car', 0.2)] ``` ::: ::: Excluding the strongest tie, `cat-dog`, forces the backbone to reach `cat` through its next best link: ::: {#bb7ec3dc .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} edges = sim.maximum_spanning_tree(return_subgraph=False, exclude=[("cat", "dog")]) [(sim.get_label_from_id(s), sim.get_label_from_id(t), w) for s, t, w in edges] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [('car', 'truck', 0.8), ('dog', 'car', 0.2), ('cat', 'car', 0.1)] ``` ::: :::
